rules.statement: When a password attempt is refused because the failed-attempt limit is reached, still verify the submitted password against a dummy hash of the current parameters, never against the stored hash, and never skip hashing.
rules.why: A refusal that skips hashing, or that checks the stored hash (possibly triggering a rehash), costs different work than a wrong password, so the response time would reveal that the limit was reached or that the password was correct.
rules.check: Look for lockout or limit branches that return early without any hash verification, or that verify the real stored hash and then refuse.

rules.statement: Count every password verification result that does not succeed, including a refusal at the attempt limit, as exactly one failed attempt under the user name the store holds, and record it with CancellationToken.None.
rules.why: A refusal should do the same work as a failed verification, one counter increment, and recording with CancellationToken.None means a cancelled request still gets counted.
rules.check: Look for refusal paths that skip RecordFailure-style calls or record them differently, and for failure recording that passes the request's cancellation token.

rules.statement: Do not let a recorded failed attempt, a refusal included, extend the expiry of the attempt-counting window; the window keeps the expiry set by its first failure.
rules.why: A refusal must cost what a wrong password costs, and the counter keeps the expiry of its first failure.
rules.check: Look for counter increments that reset or slide the expiry on every failure.

rules.statement: In a credential check, look the account up once and run the same queries whether or not the account exists; do not add database reads (such as loading claims) only when an account is found before the password is verified.
rules.why: An extra query on the found-account path is not hidden by the hash work, so timing reveals whether an account exists. A second lookup can also see a different account than the one that gets verified.
rules.check: Look for a separate lookup to resolve the counted user name, or conditional extra queries for an existing account before verification.

rules.statement: Answer a client whose password was refused at the attempt limit with the same response as a wrong password, but audit or log the refusal with its own distinct reason.
rules.why: The same response means a client cannot tell that the limit was reached or that the account exists, and the distinct audit reason lets operators tell refusals apart from wrong passwords.
rules.check: Look for distinct client-facing errors for lockout or limit refusals, or for audit entries that record a refusal as an ordinary wrong password.

rules.statement: When a pluggable store is asked whether to refuse an attempt through a callback, the caller must enforce the answer itself and fail closed: treat a success after a refusal as a refusal, and throw InvalidOperationException if the store never invoked the callback.
rules.why: This way no custom store implementation can lift the attempt limit by ignoring or skipping the refusal check.
rules.check: Look for callers that trust the store's verified result without checking the remembered limiter answer, or that accept a result when the callback was never called.
